title: She was the last woman anyone expected God to use.
paragraphs: She was the last woman anyone expected God to use.

Her city was wicked.
Her reputation was worse.
And yet… when heaven looked at Jericho, one house was marked for mercy.
Her name was Rahab.
And her story begins on a night filled with fear, whispers, and a knock at the door.
Two Israelite spies had slipped quietly into Jericho.

They were not tourists.
They were not merchants.
They were scouts from the people of God.
Jericho was already trembling with rumors. Stories had spread across the land like wildfire: the God of Israel had split the Red Sea… crushed kings… and was now marching toward Canaan.
The walls of Jericho were strong.
But the hearts inside those walls were melting.
And somehow, of all the places the spies could go… they entered Rahab’s house.
A prostitute.
A woman the “respectable” people avoided.
A woman whose life was defined by survival, compromise, and whispered shame.
But here is where the story flips.
Because God often walks straight into the houses religion refuses to enter.
That night, soldiers from the king came knocking.
“Bring out the men who came to you.”
The spies had been discovered.
Death was seconds away.
Rahab had a choice.
Protect the spies… and risk execution.
Or betray them… and save her life.
She made her decision.
Rahab rushed the men up to her roof and hid them under stalks of flax.
Then she faced the soldiers.

“They already left,” she said.
“If you hurry, you might catch them.”
The king’s men ran into the darkness chasing ghosts.
But the real miracle of the story wasn’t Rahab’s clever lie.
It was Rahab’s faith.
Before the spies left, she spoke words that shook the entire spiritual atmosphere of Jericho.
She said:
“We have heard how the Lord dried up the water of the Red Sea for you… and what you did to the kings beyond the Jordan… When we heard of it, our hearts melted.”
Then she confessed something astonishing:

“For the Lord your God, He is God in heaven above and on earth beneath.”
— Joshua 2:11
Think about that moment.
Rahab didn’t grow up in Israel.
She didn’t know the Law of Moses.
She had no spotless reputation.
But she recognized the truth when she heard it.
And faith was born.
Right there.
In the house of a prostitute.
Rahab asked the spies for mercy.
“If I have shown you kindness, swear to me by the Lord that you will also show kindness to my father’s house… spare our lives.”
The spies agreed.
But they gave her one sign.
A scarlet cord.
She was told to tie it in her window.
When Israel came to destroy Jericho, any house marked by that scarlet cord would be spared.
Don’t miss the symbolism.
A red cord hanging from a window… marking a house for salvation.
It echoes another night centuries earlier in Egypt.
When the blood of the lamb marked the doorposts and judgment passed over.
And it points forward to an even greater rescue.
The blood of Jesus Christ.
Because the deeper message of Rahab’s story is not just that she hid the spies.
It’s that God hid Rahab in grace.
When Jericho fell… every wall collapsed.
Except the section where Rahab’s house stood.
The same wall that held her shame…
became the place where God displayed His mercy.
Rahab and her family walked out alive while the city around them burned.
But God wasn’t finished with her.
Not even close.
Rahab didn’t just survive Jericho.
She became part of Israel.
Later, she married a man named Salmon.
They had a son named Boaz.
Boaz would one day marry Ruth.
Generations later… that family line produced King David.
And from David’s line came the Savior of the world:
Jesus Christ.
Let that sink in.
Rahab—the prostitute from Jericho—became part of the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:5).
God didn’t erase her story.
He redeemed it.
That’s the Gospel.
Jesus does not come for the perfect.
He comes for the repentant.
He does not build His kingdom with flawless people.
He builds it with forgiven ones.
The same grace that reached Rahab is still reaching people today.
Maybe your past feels like Jericho.
Maybe there are walls of shame, secrets, and mistakes that seem impossible to escape.
Maybe people have already labeled you.
Too broken.
Too dirty.
Too far gone.
But Rahab’s story shouts a different message.
God specializes in rescuing people from collapsing cities.
The question is not how messy your past is.
The question is:
Will you trust the God who saves?
Rahab believed.
She tied the scarlet cord.
And when judgment came, mercy found her house.
That same mercy is offered today through Jesus Christ.
His blood is the scarlet cord.
His cross is the rescue signal.
His resurrection is the proof that grace wins.
So if you feel like your life is standing on a wall that’s about to fall…
Run to Jesus.
Trust Him.
Because the God who saved Rahab still saves sinners.
And He is still rewriting stories.

From scandal…
to grace.
Someone out there needs to know that their past does not disqualify them from God’s mercy.
“We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.”
